content:
Sleeping bags in Nairobi should be chosen by the coldest night of your trip, not by price or brand. Pick a bag whose comfort rating is a few degrees below the lowest temperature you expect: around +10°C for Rift Valley camps, about 0°C for the Aberdares, and -5°C or lower for Mt Kenya.

Buying the wrong bag is one of the most common camping mistakes in Kenya. A bag that is too thin leaves you shivering at 3:00am on the moorland, while an expedition bag is heavy, bulky and wasted on a lakeside camp. This guide explains temperature ratings, down versus synthetic, shapes and sizes, what to check on a thrifted bag, how to care for it, and where to buy sleeping bags in Nairobi.

Quick Facts

  • Most important spec: the comfort temperature rating, tested under the ISO 23537 (formerly EN 13537) standard
  • Rift Valley and lakeside camps: a bag with a comfort rating of about +10°C is usually enough
  • Highland camps (Aberdares, 3,000 m and above): look for a comfort rating of about 0°C
  • Mt Kenya high camps: a comfort rating of about -5°C or lower, as summit-night camps sit above 4,000 m
  • Down vs synthetic: down is lighter and packs smaller; synthetic copes better with damp and costs less
  • Where to buy: sleeping bags in Nairobi at Mountain Mall, 3rd Floor, Shop D39, Thika Road, or online with M-Pesa or cash on delivery

What Sleeping Bag Do You Need for Camping in Kenya?

The right choice among sleeping bags in Nairobi depends on where you will camp. Low, warm sites such as Lake Naivasha suit a light bag, highland forests and moorland need a three-season bag, and Mt Kenya needs a warm four-season bag.

Kenya's camping temperatures change far more with altitude than with the calendar. Nairobi sits at about 1,795 m, and air temperature drops by roughly 6.5°C for every 1,000 m you climb, so a camp at 3,500 m can be well over 10°C colder than the city on the same night. Clear skies make it colder still, because heat escapes quickly after sunset.

How Do Sleeping Bag Temperature Ratings Work?

Sleeping bag temperature ratings tell you how cold a night the bag can handle, and they are the first thing to read when comparing sleeping bags in Nairobi. Most quality bags list three numbers, Comfort, Limit and Extreme, tested under the ISO 23537 standard, and the Comfort figure is the one to buy by.

  1. Comfort: the temperature at which a standard adult sleeper who feels the cold stays comfortable lying relaxed. Use this number when choosing.
  2. Limit (or lower limit): the temperature at which a sleeper who feels the cold less stays warm curled up for about eight hours. It is a warm sleeper's number.
  3. Extreme: a survival-only figure where there is a risk of hypothermia. Never plan a trip around it.

Some budget bags show only one large number on the label, and it is often closer to the Limit or Extreme rating than to Comfort. If a bag has no clear Comfort rating, assume it is much less warm than it looks, and choose one rated several degrees colder than you need.

Do you run cold or warm when you sleep?

If you often feel cold at night, buy a bag with a Comfort rating about 5°C lower than the coldest temperature you expect. Tiredness, hunger, altitude and damp clothes all make you feel colder, which is why Mt Kenya climbers usually need more warmth than they expect.

Down or Synthetic: Which Sleeping Bags in Nairobi Should You Choose?

Choose down if you want the lightest, most compact bag for multi-day treks and can keep it dry. Choose synthetic if you camp in wet conditions, want a lower price or are buying your first bag.

Down sleeping bags

Down sleeping bags in Nairobi give the most warmth for their weight and squash down small, which matters when you carry your own pack. Their weakness is moisture: wet down clumps and loses much of its warmth. In the Kenyan rains, pack a down bag inside a dry bag or a bin liner within your backpack.

Synthetic sleeping bags

Synthetic sleeping bags in Nairobi use polyester fibres that keep more of their warmth when damp and dry faster. They are bulkier and heavier for the same warmth, but tougher and cheaper, which makes them a sensible first bag for rainy-season camping.

Mummy, rectangular or semi-rectangular?

Most sleeping bags in Nairobi come in three shapes. A mummy bag tapers at the feet and has a hood, so there is less air for your body to heat; it is the warmest shape for cold camps. Rectangular bags are roomier and suit warm sites and restless sleepers, while semi-rectangular bags sit in between. For an example of a cold-camp design, see our post on this mummy-shape down sleeping bag.

What Should You Look for When Buying Sleeping Bags in Nairobi?

When buying sleeping bags in Nairobi, check the Comfort rating, the fill type, the length, the zip and the loft. A bag that fits your height, closes fully and springs back after compression will keep you warm for years.

What size sleeping bag should you buy?

Your sleeping bag should be long enough that your feet do not press against the end, with room for a water bottle or spare socks at the bottom, but not so long that you heat a lot of empty space. Regular sleeping bags in Nairobi usually suit people up to around 180 cm; taller campers should look for a long size. Lie in the bag in the shop if you can.

Thrifted or new sleeping bags in Nairobi?

Thrifted sleeping bags in Nairobi are good value because quality bags from respected outdoor brands are built to last a decade or more when stored properly. Our shop sells quality thrifted gear plus some new items, so a warm, branded bag can cost far less than new. Our guide to thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi covers pre-owned buying in more detail.

Do sleeping bags in Nairobi need a sleeping mat?

Yes. A sleeping mat matters as much as the bag, because the cold ground pulls heat from your back all night and your body weight flattens the insulation underneath you. Choose a mat with a higher R-value for highland and Mt Kenya camps. Add warm socks, such as our merino wool hiking socks, and a waterproof rechargeable headlamp for finding things in the tent after dark.

Pro Tips: Sleeping Warm at Camp

  • Change first: put on dry thermals and socks before you get into the bag; damp clothes chill you all night
  • Eat before bed: a warm drink and a snack help your body make heat overnight
  • Close the hood: on cold nights, pull the hood drawcord so only your face is exposed
  • Keep it dry: pack the bag in a dry bag inside your backpack during the rains
  • Air it daily: on multi-day trips, open the bag in the morning sun so body moisture can escape
  • Store it loose: at home, keep the bag in a large storage sack or hanging, never in its compression bag

How Do You Look After a Sleeping Bag?

Look after a sleeping bag by drying it fully after every trip, storing it loose rather than compressed, and washing it only when needed with a gentle, suitable detergent. Good care keeps the loft, and the loft is what keeps you warm.

Sleeping bags in Nairobi can sit unused for months between trips, so storage matters. Leaving a bag squashed in its stuff sack for months slowly crushes the fill, so it never lofts fully again. Use a liner on trips to keep body oils off the inside, which means you wash the bag itself less often. When you do wash a down bag, use a down-specific wash and dry it thoroughly on low heat or in the sun, breaking up clumps by hand.

Before camping in a national park or forest reserve, check the campsite rules and current fees with the Kenya Wildlife Service or the Kenya Forest Service. Frequently Asked Questions

What temperature sleeping bag do I need for Mt Kenya?

Mt Kenya needs a sleeping bag with a comfort rating of about -5°C or lower, because the high camps sit at around 4,200 m and nights fall below freezing. A mummy shape with a hood holds warmth best. Pair it with an insulated mat and dry thermals, and check whether your operator already provides a bag.

Is a down or synthetic sleeping bag better for Kenya?

A down sleeping bag is better for Kenyan treks where weight and pack size matter, such as Mt Kenya, provided you keep it dry. A synthetic sleeping bag is better for rainy-season camping, damp campsites and tighter budgets, because it holds more warmth when wet and costs less to replace.

How do I know if a second-hand sleeping bag is still warm?

A second-hand sleeping bag is still warm if it springs back to full thickness after a shake, the fill feels even across every section and the zip closes along its full length. Hold it up to the light to spot thin patches, and walk away from bags that smell musty or stay flat.

Can I use a sleeping bag without a sleeping mat?

A sleeping bag without a sleeping mat will feel much colder, because your body weight crushes the insulation beneath you and the ground draws heat away all night. Even a thin foam mat makes a big difference. For highland and Mt Kenya camps, use an insulated mat with a higher R-value.

Do I need a sleeping bag for camping at Lake Naivasha?

Camping at Lake Naivasha usually calls for a light sleeping bag with a comfort rating of around +10°C, because Rift Valley nights can be cool but rarely freezing. In the rainy months, a synthetic bag is the safer choice. A fleece blanket alone is often not warm enough after midnight.

Final Thoughts

Choosing sleeping bags in Nairobi is simple once you know your coldest night: buy by the Comfort rating, pick down for light treks or synthetic for wet camps, and never skip the sleeping mat. A good bag that is cared for properly will keep you warm for many years.
